The conceptual background is covered in the resource
[Object Types in R I: Functions](https://euf-methodology-hub.netlify.app/resources/r-object-types-i-functions)
on *Method and Inquiry* [@graebner2026-r-object-types-i-functions]. If any term

::: {.callout-tip}
## Where to put the code
Both functions below belong into a script in the `R` folder of your project,
e.g. `R/functions.R`, which you then make available in your analysis scripts via

```{r}
#| eval: false
here::i_am("R/analysis.R")
library(here)
source(here("R", "functions.R"))
```

This is exactly the directory structure we set up in the main session
3 — writing functions is one of the reasons why it pays off.
:::

## The golden rule

You will rarely write a function from scratch. 
The reliable recipe is usually the following:

1. **Solve the problem once** for one concrete case.
2. **Wrap** the working code into `function(){...}` and replace the concrete
   values by argument names.
3. **Test** the function on the case you already know the answer to.
4. **Generalise** it: optional arguments, defaults, a check of the input.
5. **Document** it.

Steps 1 to 3 are the important ones. If you ever find yourself writing a
function body for code you have never executed, you are doing it the hard way.

## Function 1: Fahrenheit to Celsius

A deliberately simple case: converting a temperature given in degrees Fahrenheit
into degrees Celsius. The formula is
$$T_C = \frac{5}{9}\cdot(T_F - 32)$$

### Step 1: solve it once

We pick one concrete value — the boiling point of water, 212°F — because we know
what the answer has to be:

```{r}
(5 / 9) * (212 - 32)
```

100 degrees Celsius. The code works.

### Step 2: wrap it into a function

Now we do two things: first, we put the working line into the body of a function:

```{r}
#| eval: false
fahrenheit_to_celsius <- function(){
  temp_celsius <- (5 / 9) * (212 - 32)
  return(temp_celsius)
}
```

Note that this function already works:

```{r}
fahrenheit_to_celsius()
```

But is only repeats the single case you have already covered. Therefore, 
we then replace the concrete value `212` by a **name**, which becomes the 
argument (here: `temp_fahrenheit`) and allows us to use the function for
arbitrary values:

```{r}
fahrenheit_to_celsius <- function(temp_fahrenheit){
  temp_celsius <- (5 / 9) * (temp_fahrenheit - 32)
  return(temp_celsius)
}
```

Note the four elements:

- `fahrenheit_to_celsius <-` → the **name** we assign the function to;
- `function(temp_fahrenheit)` → the **argument**, a mandatory one;
- the braces `{...}` → the **function body**, i.e. the routine;
- `return(...)` → the **output** that the function hands back.

### Step 3: test it

First on the case we already know:

```{r}
fahrenheit_to_celsius(212)
```

Then on a second one, to be sure — the freezing point, which must come out as 0:

```{r}
fahrenheit_to_celsius(temp_fahrenheit = 32)
```

Both calls do the same thing. Writing the argument name out, as in the second
call, costs a few characters and makes the code much easier to read later on.

And because R works on whole vectors, our function does too, without any extra
effort:

```{r}
fahrenheit_to_celsius(c(32, 68, 212))
```

### Step 4: the environment of the function

Inside the body we created an object called `temp_celsius`. Let us ask for it:

```{r}
temp_celsius
```

It does not exist. Every function call opens its **own environment**, and
everything created in the body lives and dies there. This is intentional: your
workspace does not fill up with the internal scrap of every function you call.

::: {.callout-note}
## Consequence for your scripts
A function can only communicate with the outside world through its
**arguments** (in) and its **return value** (out). If you want a result, you
have to return it and assign it to a name:

```{r}
boiling_point <- fahrenheit_to_celsius(212)
boiling_point
```
:::

### Step 5: document it

The convention in R is the *roxygen* style: comment lines starting with `#'`
directly above the function. A title, then the arguments via `@param`, then the
output via `@return`:

```{r}
#' Convert a temperature from degrees Fahrenheit into degrees Celsius
#'
#' @param temp_fahrenheit A number (or numeric vector) with a temperature
#'  measured in degrees Fahrenheit.
#' @return The same temperature measured in degrees Celsius.
fahrenheit_to_celsius <- function(temp_fahrenheit){
  temp_celsius <- (5 / 9) * (temp_fahrenheit - 32)
  return(temp_celsius)
}
```

This is what makes the difference between code you can reuse in six months and
code you will rewrite from scratch because you cannot remember what you did. 
Three lines of documentation per function is already a huge bargain!

## Function 2: a summary for a vector

The second function is a bit more complex. We want a compact overview of a numeric
variable — the number of observations, the mean, the standard deviation, the
minimum and the maximum — returned as a `data.frame` so that we can later stack
the results for several variables, or print them as a table.

We use a small test vector that deliberately contains a missing value:

```{r}
test_data <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42, NA)
```

### Step 1: solve it once

Again, we first write the code for this one concrete vector:

```{r}
data.frame(
  n    = length(test_data),
  mean = mean(test_data, na.rm = TRUE),
  sd   = sd(test_data, na.rm = TRUE),
  min  = min(test_data, na.rm = TRUE),
  max  = max(test_data, na.rm = TRUE)
)
```

It works — but note the inconsistency we just produced: `length()` counts the
`NA` as an observation, while the other four functions ignore it. We will fix
that in a moment. This is the normal course of events: you only see such things
once the code has run.

### Step 2: wrap it into a function

The concrete `test_data` becomes an argument called `x`, and we fix the counting
of missing values along the way:

```{r}
describe_vector <- function(x){
  x_complete <- x |> 
    tidyr::drop_na()
  
  result <- data.frame(
    n    = length(x_complete),
    mean = mean(x_complete),
    sd   = sd(x_complete),
    min  = min(x_complete),
    max  = max(x_complete)
  )
  return(result)
}

describe_vector(test_data)
```

Now `n` reports the six values the statistics are actually computed from. Note
how the local object `x_complete` lets us state the decision about missing
values **once**, instead of repeating `na.rm = TRUE` five times — that is the
*Don't Repeat Yourself* principle at work on a very small scale.

### Step 3: add an optional argument

Silently dropping missing values is a strong assumption. Usually you want to
*know* that they are there, so we make the behaviour a choice, with a default:

```{r}
describe_vector <- function(x, na.rm = TRUE){
  if (na.rm == TRUE) {
    x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  }
  result <- data.frame(
    n    = length(x),
    mean = mean(x),
    sd   = sd(x),
    min  = min(x),
    max  = max(x)
  )
  return(result)
}
```

This is what distinguishes a **mandatory** from an **optional** argument: `x`
has no default, so it must be supplied; `na.rm` has one, so it need not be:

```{r}
describe_vector(test_data)
describe_vector(test_data, na.rm = FALSE)
```

The second call returning `NA` is not a bug — it is the function telling you
that your data have holes.

### Step 4: a second optional argument

Twelve decimal places are of no use to anyone, so we add a `digits` argument,
again with a sensible default:

```{r}
describe_vector <- function(x, na.rm = TRUE, digits = 2){
  if (na.rm == TRUE) {
    x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  }
  result <- data.frame(
    n    = length(x),
    mean = mean(x),
    sd   = sd(x),
    min  = min(x),
    max  = max(x)
  )
  result <- round(result, digits = digits)
  return(result)
}

describe_vector(test_data)
describe_vector(test_data, digits = 0)
```

### Step 5: check the input

What happens if somebody — most likely future-you — hands the function something
that is not a number?

```{r}
describe_vector(c("4", "8", "15"))
```

The message complains about `Math.data.frame()`, a function that appears nowhere
in our code, and it blames the columns `min` and `max` — while the actual problem
is the input we handed over. Such messages are what makes debugging painful. So
we state our expectation about the input explicitly, right at the top of the
body:

```{r}
describe_vector <- function(x, na.rm = TRUE, digits = 2){
  stopifnot(is.numeric(x))
  if (na.rm == TRUE) {
    x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  }
  result <- data.frame(
    n    = length(x),
    mean = mean(x),
    sd   = sd(x),
    min  = min(x),
    max  = max(x)
  )
  result <- round(result, digits = digits)
  return(result)
}

describe_vector(c("4", "8", "15"))
```

Now the complaint names the actual problem. `stopifnot()` takes one or more
conditions and stops the function as soon as one of them is not `TRUE`.

### Step 6: the finished function

Documented, this is the version that goes into `R/functions.R`:

```{r}
#' Compute summary statistics for a numeric vector
#'
#' Computes the number of observations, the mean, the standard deviation, the
#'  minimum and the maximum of a numeric vector and returns them as a one-row
#'  data frame.
#'
#' @param x A numeric vector to be described.
#' @param na.rm Logical. Should missing values be removed before the statistics
#'  are computed? Default is `TRUE`.
#' @param digits The number of decimal places to which the results are rounded.
#'  Default is `2`.
#' @return A `data.frame` with one row and the columns `n`, `mean`, `sd`, `min`
#'  and `max`.
describe_vector <- function(x, na.rm = TRUE, digits = 2){
  stopifnot(is.numeric(x))
  if (na.rm == TRUE) {
    x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  }
  result <- data.frame(
    n    = length(x),
    mean = mean(x),
    sd   = sd(x),
    min  = min(x),
    max  = max(x)
  )
  result <- round(result, digits = digits)
  return(result)
}
```

And this is why it was worth the effort — describing three variables is now
three lines of readable code:

```{r}
rbind(
  Sepal.Length = describe_vector(iris$Sepal.Length),
  Sepal.Width  = describe_vector(iris$Sepal.Width),
  Petal.Length = describe_vector(iris$Petal.Length)
)
```

## Your turn

Two exercises to make sure the recipe sticks. Use the five steps from above, and
do not skip step 1.

1. Write a function `celsius_to_fahrenheit()` that reverses function 1, and
   check that `celsius_to_fahrenheit(fahrenheit_to_celsius(212))` gives you
   `212` back.
2. Extend `describe_vector()` by an optional argument `median` (default
   `FALSE`); if it is set to `TRUE`, the returned data frame contains an
   additional column with the median of `x`.

If you want more practice, the exercise set `Functions` from the
`DataScienceExercises` package is exactly about this:

```{r}
#| eval: false
learnr::run_tutorial(
  name = "Functions",
  package = "DataScienceExercises",
  shiny_args = list("launch.browser" = TRUE))
```
